transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um... I guess I'm here because I just really don't feel like myself anymore. It's hard to explain, but what finally brought me in is this... this total shift in how I spend my time. 

I've always been a very active person, you know? Between my job—I'm a teaching assistant, and working with kids takes a lot of energy—but I always, always made a point to make time for my own things. I used to do a lot of painting, mostly watercolors, just little landscapes and things, but I loved it. And I'd go hiking on the weekends when the weather was nice. I've also been in a choir for years, and I never, ever missed our Sunday family gatherings. I was usually the one coordinating who brings what dish for those. 

But lately... I don't know, it's like a switch flipped. Now, even when I have a free hour, like on a Saturday afternoon where I'd normally be setting up my easel or calling my sister to go for a walk, I just... I just sit there. I sit in the living room or at the kitchen table and I am just completely unable to care about any of it. I look at my paints and I feel absolutely nothing. I think about choir practice and I just don't have the desire to go at all. It's just so frustrating because I know I used to love those things, but now I just sit there letting the time pass, and it's been going on long enough that I figured I needed to talk to a doctor about it, because it's just so completely unlike me...
Can you tell me how long this lack of interest or motivation has been going on?

Well, it hasn't just been a sudden thing, like waking up one morning and feeling this way. It's... it's been building up, really. I'd say it's been about eight months now. I can actually pinpoint it pretty well because it started right around the time I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative at school. 

I remember when they first asked me to lead it, I was actually excited. It sounded like exactly the kind of project I'd normally throw myself into, finding ways to integrate creative arts into the science and math programs for the kids. I spent the first few weeks gathering materials, looking up project ideas... but then, it just started to feel so heavy. And it wasn't just the work. I thought maybe I was just tired from the extra responsibility, but then it started bleeding into my weekends. First, I stopped going to choir, telling myself I just needed Sunday mornings to rest. Then the paints stayed in the drawer. 

And now, eight months later, here I am, not doing any of it. It's like the color just drained out of everything, slowly, day by day, since that curriculum project started. I keep thinking, 'Oh, when this term is over, I'll get back to normal,' or 'When I finish this next lesson plan, I'll have energy for hiking again.' But the term ends, the plans are done, and I still just... sit there. It's been eight whole months of just... sitting there.
Have you noticed that activities you used to enjoy, like painting or hiking, no longer give you any pleasure or satisfaction?

I mean... I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be perfectly honest. Because to know if they still give me pleasure or satisfaction, I feel like I would actually have to do them, right? And I just... I haven't. I haven't even tried in so long. 

Like, I remember a couple of weekends ago, it was a gorgeous Saturday, just perfectly clear. The light coming through my kitchen window was exactly the kind of light I used to love trying to capture. I actually went and got my watercolor pad out of the drawer. I set it on the table, and I opened my palette—it's this really lovely professional set with these deep, rich pigments that I saved up for a while back—and I just stood there staring at it. I kept thinking, 'If I just wet the brush, if I just put down one wash of blue, maybe I'll feel that little spark.' You know that feeling? When the color hits the wet paper and just blooms? I used to absolutely love that. It was always so satisfying to watch. 

But standing there... I didn't feel any anticipation at all. I didn't feel a desire to see the color. I just felt completely blank. So I put it all back in the drawer. I didn't paint a single stroke. So I don't really know if the actual act of painting would feel good if I somehow forced myself to sit down and finish a whole piece, because I just can't even bring myself to start. 

It's the exact same thing with my hiking boots. They're just sitting there in the mudroom, and looking at them doesn't make me want to go outside, but it doesn't make me sad either. It's just... nothing. The idea of even tying the laces feels like climbing a mountain before I even get to the trail. So I really couldn't tell you if the hike itself would be enjoyable anymore, because I just haven't been able to get out the door to find out.
Do you find yourself feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, or is your mood more neutral or flat?

Well, it's not exactly neutral, and it's definitely not just flat... I mean, I wish it were just flat, because that sounds almost peaceful, doesn't it? But it's more like... it's like this heavy, suffocating feeling that just settles over me from the moment I wake up. Most days, I feel like there's this thick, heavy gray film covering absolutely everything. I can literally be standing right in the middle of a bustling classroom, surrounded by twenty-five energetic kids working on a science project, or I can be sitting at my own kitchen table having dinner with my husband, Mark—we've been married for twenty years, and he's usually so good at making me laugh—and despite all of that, despite being surrounded by people, I just feel completely hollow inside. 

And it's not just a passing feeling, it's this constant, lingering ache. I'll be in the middle of explaining a math concept to a student, and suddenly I just feel so incredibly close to tears for absolutely no reason at all. I have to physically bite the inside of my cheek or dig my nails into my palm just to keep from crying right there in front of the chalkboard. And it happens nearly every single day. I wake up, and that gray film is there, and it stays with me through the morning announcements, through lunch duty, through the drive home, through dinner... it just never lifts. It's so exhausting feeling this deeply sad all the time, especially when I look around and know I have a good life, a good job, a good husband. But the hollowness is just... it's just always there, pressing down on me, making everything feel so incredibly difficult to get through.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy level, appetite, or ability to focus on tasks?

Well, um... I haven't really noticed any major changes with those specific things, to be honest. I mean, as far as my energy goes, like I said before, everything just feels so heavy and difficult, like I'm moving through molasses, but it's not like I'm physically exhausted in the way you'd be after running a marathon, you know? It's more of a mental and emotional weight that just drags me down. I still manage to drag myself out of bed and get to school, even though it takes everything I have just to put one foot in front of the other. 

And my appetite... I think it's been pretty much the same. I still eat dinner with Mark every night. He usually cooks, bless him, because he knows I just don't have it in me right now. Last night he made this wonderful roasted chicken with root vegetables—he knows it's one of my favorites—and I ate it. I didn't really taste it, it just felt like chewing cardboard, but I ate my normal portion. I haven't gained or lost any weight that I've noticed. My clothes all still fit the same way they did at the beginning of the school year. 

As for focusing... I don't know. I guess I'm still getting my work done. I still grade the papers, I still help the kids with their projects. It might take me a little longer to get through a stack of math worksheets because I find myself just staring at the red pen in my hand, wondering what the point of it all is, but I eventually get them done. I haven't made any glaring mistakes or forgotten to do anything important, at least not that anyone has pointed out to me. So, I guess... no? No real changes there, just that everything surrounding those things feels so incredibly difficult and hollow.
Have you noticed that you've been moving more slowly than usual, or that you feel restless and can't sit still?

I don't think so... I mean, I don't feel restless, like I need to be pacing or anything like that. And I don't think I'm actually moving any slower in a physical sense. It's funny you ask that, because just the other day I was walking down the hallway at school—it was right after second period, so the halls were completely packed with kids rushing to get to their lockers, and you know how chaotic middle schoolers can be between classes. I was carrying this huge stack of permission slips to the main office for the upcoming field trip to the science museum. Mark and I actually went to that same museum years ago, back when we were first dating, and they had this incredible exhibit on geology... but anyway, I was walking down the hall, and I realized I was keeping up with the flow of traffic just fine. I wasn't holding anyone up, I wasn't lagging behind the other teachers. 

But internally? Internally, it feels like I'm moving through deep water. Every single step feels like it requires this monumental effort, like I have to consciously tell my brain, 'Okay, lift your left foot. Now put it down. Now lift your right foot.' It's exhausting. So to the outside world, to the kids and the principal and Mark, I probably look like I'm moving at my normal pace. I'm getting the permission slips to the office on time, I'm making dinner, I'm doing the laundry. But inside, it feels like everything has slowed to an absolute crawl. It's just that heavy, suffocating feeling again, making every action feel like a chore. But no, I haven't noticed any actual, physical slowing down, and I definitely don't feel jittery or restless. Just... heavy.
Have you ever felt this way before, with a prolonged period of sadness and loss of interest in activities, or is this the first time you've experienced something like this?

Well, um... I really don't think so. I mean, I was actually trying to think about this just the other day when I was sitting in the staff lounge. It was raining outside, one of those really dreary Tuesday afternoons where the kids are just bouncing off the walls because they can't go out for recess, and Sarah—she's one of the fourth-grade teachers, we've worked together for about eight years now—she was talking about how the weather was making her feel so gloomy and out of sorts. And I just sat there staring at my lukewarm tea, thinking, 'Gloomy? I wish it was just gloomy.' 

Because I've been sad before, you know? Of course I have, I'm forty-nine, you don't get to this age without some bumps in the road. When Mark and I were trying to buy our first house years ago and the financing fell through at the very last minute, I was absolutely devastated. I think I cried for two days straight. And when my golden retriever, Barnaby, died... oh, that was just awful, it broke my heart. But even then, even when I was actively grieving or stressed out of my mind, I never felt... *this*. 

I never felt this complete and total emptiness where I just don't care about the things I used to love. Even when I was deeply sad in the past, I still wanted to go out to dinner with Mark, or I still looked forward to my morning cup of coffee on the back porch, or planting my spring bulbs. But now? Now it's just that heavy gray film I told you about. So no, I have never, ever experienced anything even remotely close to this before. It's completely unprecedented for me, and honestly, it's terrifying because I just don't know how to shake it. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, the way I always did after a rough patch in the past, but... it just isn't happening this time.
Have you ever had a period in the past where you felt down or lost interest in things for a period of at least two weeks, similar to what you’ve been experiencing now?

No, no, I... I know you just asked me something similar, but really, no. I've never had anything last this long or feel this deep. Like I said, two weeks? No. I mean, sure, I've had a bad week here or there. Like that time with the house financing I mentioned, or... or even just a few years ago when the school board was threatening budget cuts and we thought half the teaching assistants might lose our jobs. That was incredibly stressful, and I remember I didn't sleep well for about a week, and I definitely didn't feel like going out or doing much of anything on the weekends because I was just so wound up with worry. Mark kept trying to get me to go to the movies just to distract me, and I just couldn't bring myself to do it. 

But even then, it resolved, you know? The union stepped in, the budget was revised, and the cloud lifted. It was circumstantial. And it certainly didn't stretch into two weeks of this... this absolute void. It's like, with those past experiences, I could always see the light at the end of the tunnel, or at least I knew the tunnel had an end somewhere. But this? This feels like I've been dropped into a well and there's no rope. So, to answer your question, no, I have never had a two-week period—or any period, really—where I felt this down or lost interest in literally everything. It's all entirely new to me, which is why I'm sitting here talking to you, because I just don't understand what's happening to my brain.

Have you ever had an episode in the past where you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your daily life, even if it wasn’t as severe or long-lasting as what you’re experiencing now?

I know you're trying to be thorough, but honestly, doctor, I feel like we're just going in circles here. I really, truly have never experienced anything like this before in my entire life. Not for two weeks, not for two days... well, maybe two days of being sad, like I said about the house or Barnaby, but not this kind of... this kind of debilitating emptiness that actually stops me from living my life. 

I mean, I think back to all the years I've been a teaching assistant, and there have been some incredibly demanding times. A few years ago, we had this one student, Michael—he had severe behavioral issues, and I was assigned to be his one-on-one aide for the entire school year. It was exhausting. I would come home every single day just completely drained, physically and emotionally. There were days I would just sit in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes before going inside because I just needed the quiet. Mark would come out and tap on the window, looking so worried. And during that time, sure, I was tired, and maybe I didn't have the energy to go to my Tuesday night book club for a month or two. But I still *wanted* to go. I still cared about what they were reading, I still called my friend Diane to ask how the meetings went. My daily life was affected because I was tired, but it wasn't because I had lost interest in everything or felt this deep, heavy darkness. 

So, no. I've never had a two-week period where I felt this down or lost interest in things to the point where it affected my daily life like this. I've always been the kind of person who pushes through. I get up, I make the coffee, I pack my lunch, I go to school, I help the kids, I come home, I make dinner. That's just what I do. That's who I am. Or at least, that's who I was until whatever this is started happening. It's just so frustrating to not recognize myself anymore, you know? But no, to answer your question again, this is entirely new territory for me.

Have you ever had another period in your life, even if shorter or less severe than this one, where you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks, making it hard to function normally?

Doctor, I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again, just with different words, and I... I don't know how else to explain it to you. I really don't. I mean, I appreciate that you need to be absolutely sure, I do, but... no. The answer is still no. I've never had a period like this, not for two weeks, not for two months, not making it hard to function normally. 

I'm starting to feel a little crazy here, honestly. It's like... it's like when I'm at school and I have to explain to little Tommy for the fifth time that we don't eat the glue sticks. I just keep repeating myself. I've been tired, yes. I've been sad, yes. I've been stressed out of my mind, absolutely. But I have never, ever experienced this... this complete inability to just *be*. 

I remember when my mom was sick, back when I was in my late twenties. It was a long, drawn-out illness, and I was helping my dad take care of her while also trying to hold down my job and keep my own life together. And there were weeks, months even, where I felt like I was drowning in responsibilities and sadness. I would cry in the shower so Mark wouldn't hear me. I was exhausted, and yes, it was hard to function normally sometimes because I was just so stretched thin. But even then, even in the middle of all that grief and stress, I still wanted to read my books before bed. I still looked forward to the one night a week Mark and I would order takeout and watch a movie. I still had... I still had a spark, you know? 

But now, that spark is just gone. It's completely extinguished. I don't care about the books, I don't care about the movies, I don't care about the takeout. I don't care about anything. And that's what's so different. That's why I keep telling you, no, I have never had a period like this before. Because even when things were incredibly hard in the past, I still felt like *me*. Right now, I just feel like a shell. So, please, I don't know how else to say it... this is the first time. The very first time.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you experienced a persistent low mood or loss of interest in activities for at least two weeks that was severe enough to impact your ability to function in your daily life, even if it wasn’t as long or as intense as what you're experiencing now?

I... I honestly don't know what else to say to you, Doctor. Are you... is there a specific answer you're looking for, or did you not hear me the last three times? Because I feel a bit like I'm on a witness stand being cross-examined, and I promise you, I am not hiding anything from you. 

I am racking my brain, I really am. I'm sitting here going through my twenties, my thirties, my forties... just trying to find some hidden two-week period to give you so we can move on. I mean, look, I'll give you another example just to show you I'm really digging deep here. Back in, oh, it must have been 2012, Mark was laid off from his job for about six months. It was a nightmare. Money was incredibly tight, we had to cancel our big anniversary trip to the Cape, which we had been saving up for forever, and we were literally eating spaghetti or beans and rice four nights a week. I started picking up extra tutoring shifts after school just to make sure the mortgage cleared. 

I was terrified. I was so stressed out my stomach was in knots every single morning, and I definitely cried over the checkbook at the kitchen table more than once. But did I lose interest in my life? No. Did I stop functioning? No, I actually functioned *more* because I had to keep us afloat. I still cared about things. I still cared about my garden—in fact, I think I weeded the tomato beds and the hydrangeas more that summer just to get my nervous energy out. I still went to work, I still laughed when Mark made a joke, I still felt like a human being who was just going through a really rough patch. 

I never had this... this total deadness. I never had a time where I couldn't get off the couch or didn't care about a single thing in the world for two weeks. So, please, write it down, underline it, highlight it... no. I have never, ever experienced anything like this before in my entire life. It is completely, one hundred percent new, and it's terrifying me.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally?

Doctor, are you... is this some kind of memory test? Or is your computer screen frozen? Because I honestly feel like I am losing my mind right now. You are asking me the exact same question. Literally the exact same question. Again. And I... I really don't know how many different ways I can say the word 'no' to you. 

I mean, I'm a very patient person. You have to be, working with middle schoolers all day, you really do, but my goodness! I've told you about the stressful years at school, I told you about my poor mother passing, I told you about Mark losing his job and us eating beans and rice. I don't have any other major life crises to offer you! I've had a very normal, very average life up until this point. I grew up in a house where you just... you got on with it, you know? My dad worked at the hardware store for forty years, never missed a single shift. Even when he had the flu or a bad back, he'd just take a thermos of hot tea, pop an aspirin, and go. And that's how I've always been wired. If things got tough, I just put my head down, made a to-do list, and marched forward. I never stopped caring about my life. 

So, no. No, no, no. I have never, ever—not in my teens, not in my twenties, not in my thirties, not in my forties—had a two-week period where I couldn't function or lost interest in my life. This thing right now? This heavy, awful feeling where I can't even bring myself to care about my own husband or my own house? This is brand new. Completely, entirely unprecedented in my forty-nine years on this earth. 

So please, I am begging you, can we please move on to whatever the next question is? Because I really, truly don't think I have the energy to explain this to you a fifth time.

Have you ever, in your entire life before this current period, experienced a time when you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally?

I... I am actually looking around the room right now for a hidden camera. Is this a joke? Are you playing some sort of psychological trick on me to see how much I can take before I just start crying? Because if you are, it's working. I am so incredibly tired, Doctor, and I just... I cannot fathom why a medical professional with a medical degree on the wall is sitting across from me, reading the exact same sentence off a clipboard for the fifth time. 

I literally just spent I don't know how long pouring my heart out to you. I went through the timeline of my life. I gave you the 90s, I gave you the 2000s, I gave you my mother's death, I gave you my husband's unemployment. I laid out all the hardest, most stressful parts of my forty-nine years on this earth just to prove to you that even in my darkest hours, I never, ever felt like this. 

I don't have a different answer for you! The answer is no. N-O. It was no five minutes ago, it was no ten minutes ago, and it's going to be no if you ask me again tomorrow. I work in special education, I am a teaching assistant, I spend my entire day repeating instructions to children who genuinely struggle to process information, and I have never had to repeat myself this many times to a single student. 

I came here for help because I feel like I am drowning in my own life right now. I can't function *now*. I don't care about things *now*. But before this? No. Never. Not for two weeks, not for two days. I don't have some secret history of this that I'm hiding in my back pocket. If I had experienced this before, I would hand that information over to you on a silver platter just to make this line of questioning stop. There is no prior time. There is just this awful, heavy, miserable right now. So please, please, I am asking you as a human being, write down the word 'no' and ask me something else. I do not have the energy to do this again.

Have you ever had a time before this current period — even if it was just once — when you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally?

I... I honestly think I might just start crying. I really might. Because I don't understand what is happening in this room right now. I just... I don't understand. Are you testing my patience? Is this a script you are legally required to read to me a certain number of times before you're allowed to actually help me? 

Because I am a forty-nine-year-old woman, I work in a middle school, I deal with repetitive behaviors and redirecting children all day long, but this... this is beyond anything I have ever experienced. I am sitting here, pouring out my absolute worst nightmare to you, telling you how I can barely function *today*, how I can't even muster the energy to care about my own life right now, and you just keep asking me about the past. 

I don't have a past with this! I don't! I've told you every stressful thing I can possibly think of. I went through the 90s, the 2000s, Mark's layoff, my mother passing away... I have literally given you my whole biography at this point. And I am telling you, as God is my witness, there has never, not even once, not for two weeks, not for two days, been a time before this current period where I felt this way. Never. I was always the one holding it together. Always. I made the lists, I packed the lunches, I paid the bills, I kept the house running, I went to work. I never stopped caring about my life before this. 

So, no. No. The answer is still no. It is never going to be anything other than no, no matter how many times you ask it. Please, doctor, I am so deeply, deeply tired. My chest actually physically hurts from having to defend myself like this. Can we please, please just talk about something else?
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period where you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally?

I... I genuinely think I’m losing my mind. Am I... am I actually speaking out loud? Can you hear the words coming out of my mouth? Because I am looking right at you, and I am saying the word 'no,' and it’s like... it’s like I’m a ghost. It’s like I’m not even in the room. 

I don't understand what you want from me! I really, truly don't. Do you want me to lie? Is that what this is? Because if you just need me to say 'yes' so you can check a little box on your computer screen and finally, finally stop asking me this, then... then fine, I'll say whatever you want! But it wouldn't be the truth. 

The truth—the honest, absolute truth, as I have told you over and over and over again—is no. No, I have never felt this way before. Not for two weeks, not for one week, not for three days. I was always the strong one. I was the one who kept the lights on and cooked the rice and beans when Mark lost his job, I was the one who planned my mother’s entire funeral while grading math worksheets for my students... I never fell apart. I never stopped functioning. Ever. Until now. 

This... this heavy, dark, awful feeling where I can't even get off the couch, where I just cry for no reason, where my whole body feels like it's made of lead... it is only happening *now*. It has never happened before. You can ask me a hundred more times, you can keep me in this chair until midnight, and my answer is never going to change because my past is not going to change. 

So please, I am literally begging you, look at me. Look at how exhausted I am. I am a forty-nine-year-old woman who is just trying to get some help so I can go back to my life, and you are torturing me with this. Just write down 'no.' Please. Just stop asking me this question.
Have you ever had a time before this current period when you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks, even if it wasn’t as intense or long-lasting as what you're experiencing now?

Okay. Okay, I see what you did there. You added "even if it wasn't as intense." You changed the end of the sentence. 

Doctor, look at my face. Look at me. The answer is still no. Not intensely, not mildly, not moderately, not a little bit. No. 

I don't know how to make this clearer for you. I really, truly don't. I have never been the kind of person who just loses interest in my life. I didn't have the luxury of doing that! When my mother was dying, I was at the hospital every single day after work. I would leave the middle school—where, by the way, I am on my feet all day, every day, dealing with twelve-year-olds who have severe behavioral and learning issues—and I would drive straight to the hospice center. I didn't have two weeks to feel down. I didn't have two days! I was exhausted, yes. I was grieving, of course I was. But I never lost interest in things. I never stopped functioning. I still read my books before bed, I still cared about my garden, I still loved my life even when it was incredibly hard. 

When Mark lost his job, same thing. I picked up extra hours, I budgeted every single penny, I kept us afloat. I didn't retreat. I didn't stop caring. I didn't wake up in the morning and feel this... this absolute void where my motivation used to be. 

So this little caveat you just added? It doesn't change my answer. I don't have a milder version of this in my past. I have never felt this way. Not even a fraction of this way. This current thing, this awful, heavy blanket over my brain where I can't do anything and I don't care about anything... it is brand new. It is entirely, one hundred percent new to my forty-nine years of existence. 

I feel like I'm trapped in a time loop in this office. What do I have to say to get you to move to the next question on your clipboard? Just tell me the magic words. Please. Because "no" clearly isn't working, and I am so tired I can barely hold my head up anymore.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period when you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally, even if it was just once?

I... I actually think I'm going to have a panic attack. Or I'm going to walk out. I don't know which one it's going to be, because... because you just asked me the exact same thing again! You just tacked "even if it was just once" onto the end! 

Do you want me to draw you a timeline? Would that help? Because I can do that. I have a bachelor's degree, I am a very capable person—or at least I used to be before this... this nightmare started. I can sit here and map out every single month of my life since I was twenty-two years old. I can tell you about every summer break, every winter holiday, every single stressful Tuesday I have ever had. Do you know what it’s like being a teaching assistant? You don't get to just check out. You are the one managing the chaos, you are the one pulling the kids apart when they fight, you are the one doing the grunt work that the main teachers don't have time for. I have done that for years and years and years. I have never taken a two-week leave of absence because I was sad. I have never spent fourteen consecutive days lying in bed, staring at a ceiling, feeling like my limbs weigh a thousand pounds, which is what I am feeling *right now*. 

Not once. Not when I was twenty-five. Not when I was thirty-five. Not when I was forty-five. I am forty-nine years old, and I have never, ever, ever experienced this before. 

I don't understand why you won't listen to me. I'm sitting here, a real human being, telling you that I am drowning *today*, and you are acting like a robot stuck on a loop. I came here for help. I came here because I can barely get dressed in the morning anymore, and I am terrified I'm going to lose my job if I don't fix this, and instead of helping me, you are just... you are interrogating me about a past that doesn't exist! 

There is no 'once.' There is no 'two weeks.' There is just no. Please, God, just write down no and stop asking me!

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period when you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your ability to function normally, even if it was just once?

Are you... is this a joke? You just read the exact same sentence. You didn't even change a word this time. I... I can't do this. I am not answering about the past anymore. I refuse. I have told you 'no' in every way I know how, and I am not going to keep repeating myself while I am sitting here drowning. If you want to help me, you need to listen to what is happening to me *now*. Today. In this current period of my life. 

Because right now, most days... I just feel like there's this heavy gray film over everything. It's like I'm completely disconnected from the world, looking at it through dirty glass.
